p: FDA asks how much potential a change has to have an adverse effect on the identity, strength, quality, purity or potency of the product, as these relate to its safety or effectiveness. Substantial potential makes a major change; moderate potential a moderate change; minimal potential a minor change.
The same three tests apply to NDAs and ANDAs (21 CFR 314.70, applied to ANDAs by 314.97) and to BLAs (21 CFR 601.12).
Prior approval supplement (PAS): major changes. Product made with the change is distributed only after FDA approves.
Supplement - Changes Being Effected in 30 Days (CBE-30): moderate changes. Distribution can start 30 days after FDA receives the supplement, unless FDA says otherwise in that time.
Supplement - Changes Being Effected (CBE-0): moderate changes FDA allows at once. Distribution can start when FDA receives the supplement.
Annual report (AR): minor changes. Make the change, then describe it in the next annual report, due within 60 days of the anniversary of approval.

sections.h: Do and tell, or tell and wait
p: The app shows a badge on every result: do and tell (annual report), tell then do at once (CBE-0), tell, wait 30 days, then do (CBE-30), or wait for approval (PAS). It is the first thing a change control board needs to know.

When related changes are filed together, use the most restrictive category of the individual changes (guidance section XII). Unrelated changes can go separately, so a minor change does not have to wait for a major one.

A move to a site that FDA has never inspected for the type of operation, or that restarts an operation stopped for more than two years, is a prior approval supplement (VI.B.1). So is a move to a site without a satisfactory CGMP inspection for that operation (VI.B.2).

Some products make a move major even to a good site: modified-release products, products whose primary packaging controls the dose (VI.B.3), aseptic processing into a new or dissimilar area (VI.B.4) and terminally sterilized products into a newly built facility at a different site (VI.B.5).
Otherwise a move is a CBE-30 (VI.C.1.a), with special cases for aseptic areas that already make similar products (VI.C.1.b), primary packaging (VI.C.1.c) and testing labs (VI.C.1.d).
Secondary packaging, labeling, ink imprinting and early intermediates are annual report items (VI.D).

A change of technology (wet to dry granulation, a new drying method, a new synthetic route) is a prior approval supplement (VII.B.4). So are changes that may affect controlled release (VII.B.1) or sterility assurance (VII.B.2).

Other changes to process, parameters or equipment are CBE-30 (VII.C.1.a). Equipment of the same design and operating principle, and changes in scale, are annual report items (VII.D.1) unless another rule applies.

The 2004 guidance keeps the SUPAC categories for components and composition. For immediate-release solids, SUPAC-IR Level 1 changes are annual report items; Levels 2 and 3 need prior approval, Level 3 usually with an in vivo bioequivalence study.

Tightening a limit is minor (VIII.D.3). Adding a test that increases assurance is a CBE-0 (VIII.C.2.a). Relaxing a limit or deleting a test needs prior approval (VIII.B.1, VIII.B.2), except where it follows a compendium (CBE-30, VIII.C.1.e) or concerns early raw materials (CBE-30, VIII.C.1.b).

A new regulatory procedure, or one that gives less assurance, needs prior approval (VIII.B.3, VIII.B.4). Other changes to a regulatory procedure are CBE-30. Alternative procedures with the same or greater assurance are annual report items (VIII.D.2).

sections.h: Most labeling changes need prior approval
p: 21 CFR 314.70(b)(2)(v) makes labeling changes prior approval supplements, except the safety and editorial changes the rule lists. New indications and population changes come as efficacy supplements with clinical data.

Adding or strengthening a contraindication, warning, precaution or adverse reaction, an instruction for safer use, or deleting misleading claims can go in at once as a CBE-0, when based on newly acquired information with reasonable evidence of a causal association (314.70(c)(6)(iii); 601.12(f)(2) for biologics).

If FDA becomes aware of new safety information that it believes should be in the labeling, it notifies the holder. The holder has 30 days to submit a supplement with the change or a statement of why it is not warranted; disagreements follow a set timetable, after which FDA can order the change.
ANDA labeling must be the same as the reference listed drug's, apart from permitted differences, so generic holders update their labeling when the brand's changes.

A comparability protocol (FDA's name for a post-approval change management protocol under ICH Q12) describes a future change, the studies and the acceptance criteria. It is approved first, in a prior approval supplement; afterwards the change it covers can be filed in the lower category it sets.

FDA's 2021 guidance for certain biological products treats many process, facility and specification changes as prior approval: new master cell banks, new purification steps or resins, viral clearance changes. The app shows when a result comes from guidance written for small molecules.

ICH Q12 lets a holder agree with FDA which elements are established conditions. Changes to other elements are managed in the quality system without a filing. The app adds established conditions and the product lifecycle management document in a later phase.
